papers.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions

papers.title: Mission (Im)Possible: Towards Autonomous Discovery of Autopilot Logic Flaws in Open-Source Drone Frameworks
papers.abstract: Autonomous drones are increasingly deployed in safety-critical tasks, yet their autopilot software can still contain subtle logic flaws that lead to unsafe behaviors. These flaws are difficult to discover with existing techniques because they often depend on semantic relationships across modules, commands, and runtime state, and rarely manifest as crashes or detectable failures. With recent advances in LLMs, we observe that, when equipped with essential domain knowledge and carefully crafted context, LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in understanding the high-level semantics of autopilot systems, making them suitable for logic flaw discovery. However, LLMs are limited by their context and can be biased to the vulnerabilities frequently occurs in training dataset, while logic flaws often require higher-level semantic bug oracles to identify their existence. papers.title: BenchChecker: Assessing the Credibility of Bug-Fixing Benchmarks for LLMs
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for Automatic Program Repair (APR), existing benchmarks suffer from data contamination, in which test samples appear in training sets, artificially inflating performance. To address this, we propose BenchChecker, a framework compatible with both open-source and closed-source models that supports more credible evaluation by detecting such contamination. Grounded in the observation that persistent patches likely remain in recent repository snapshots used for training, BenchChecker employs a forensics-based two-stage detection process using only textual model outputs together with public repository history. papers.title: STP-GUI: Spatially-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Web-GUI Agents
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. papers.title: Look Before You Restore: Learning to Predict Before Acting for Agentic Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. papers.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. papers.title: Reliability-Aware Multimodal Sentiment Prediction Under Local Modality Missingness
papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment models are usually evaluated on complete utterances, yet streams often lose a contiguous span of text, audio, or video. We study local missingness on aligned CMU-MOSEI features. Our reliability-aware network (RM-Net) keeps the original temporal positions, represents unobserved positions with a learned token, outputs bounded per-modality intensity contributions gated by observation quality, and is trained with dual-view masking of contiguous segments. We fuse five RM-Net seeds with a LoRA-adapted BERT text expert, using a fusion weight that depends only on the visible fraction of content tokens. Architecture, checkpoint, and fusion choices were made on the validation split. papers.title: OLiVES: An Outdoor Low-Light Video Benchmark for Enhancement and Segmentation
papers.abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). papers.title: BluePixel: Toward Native 4K Agentic Image Editing
papers.abstract: Instruction-driven image editing has reached native 4K, yet how such editors are trained remains undisclosed, and pretraining one from scratch is beyond most teams. The task itself compounds the difficulty: a single end-to-end editor cannot make precise parametric adjustments, match specialized experts, or interpret the vague instructions users actually write. We argue that 4K editing is a system problem rather than a single-model problem, and present BluePixel, which couples a native-4K editing model with an agent harness; the complete training recipe is disclosed in this paper. The model makes 4K training practical: it turns a 1K-pretrained editor into a native-4K one through progressive VAE adaptation that keeps 4K training as affordable as 1K, absorbs a long tail of vertical editing skills through continual learning, and refines the aesthetic-fidelity trade-off with reinforcement lea

papers.title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
papers.abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). papers.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding
papers.abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. papers.title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding
papers.abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. papers.title: Why Do VLMs Fail at Remote Physiological Measurement? Rethinking with Physiological Grounding and Numerical Alignment
papers.abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. papers.title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. papers.title: SaTPO: Text-to-Image Safety Alignment via Transition Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of text-to-image diffusion models aims to suppress harmful content without compromising useful generation capabilities. However, preferences over completed images compress multidimensional generation factors into a coarse signal, potentially driving changes beyond those required for safety. To address this, we propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO), which enforces step-wise alignment during denoising. SaTPO leverages the insight that an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form a tightly coupled preference pair when conditioned on a shared parent state and noise realization. By anchoring optimization on identical parent states, SaTPO eliminates historical trajectory divergence, confining safety adaptation to an incremental alignment while preserving task-relevant semantics. papers.title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
papers.abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. papers.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
papers.abstract: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. papers.title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
papers.abstract: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. papers.title: Defense Filters for Robust Learning of Partially Observed Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Robust estimation of unknown system dynamics from partial observations under attack is a core challenge in learning for control, increasingly critical in multi-agent networks subject to adversarial data poisoning. Existing methods either require highly restrictive assumptions on the adversary or yield weak error bounds. In this paper, we consider identifying partially observed linear dynamical systems subject to adversarial attacks with an attack probability $p < 0.5$ at each time. We propose a defense-filtering framework in which a system designer leverages knowledge of the observation matrix to construct a defense filter satisfying full column rank and subspace separability conditions, which enables the evaluation of a single-attack scenario against observed data. papers.title: Receiver-Specific Interventional Valuation of Semantic Atoms for Budget-Constrained Multi-Agent Communication
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent semantic communication requires deciding not only how a transmitter encodes its observation, but also which resulting semantic content should be delivered to each receiver under a limited link budget. We introduce an encoder-agnostic transmitter-side framework for receiver-specific valuation of independently selectable semantic units, termed semantic atoms. Each atom is assigned a signed value that quantifies whether delivering it is expected to improve or degrade the intended receiver's downstream decision. We formulate this effect through a controlled-delivery utility and identify it via prospective randomized payload delivery before the receiver acts. papers.title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. papers.title: ConStore: Search-Overlapped Prefetch and Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Storage for Disk-Based ANNS
papers.abstract: Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search, recommendation, and advertising over corpora that exceed memory capacity. Existing ANNS research often focuses on vector search at small top-K, whereas industrial-scale applications require larger retrieval sets. Fetching the corresponding content from storage remains comparatively underexplored. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector corpora shows that, at large K, content fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency and cannot be ignored in end-to-end retrieval. We present ConStore, a content storage engine combining two complementary techniques to reduce end-to-end retrieval latency. papers.title: From One Query to Many: A Critical Survey of Privacy Accounting in RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models to leverage external knowledge but introduces privacy risks when the retrieved corpus contains sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, yet interpreting and comparing privacy guarantees across existing DP-RAG methods remains challenging. In particular, a privacy budget reported for a single response does not directly characterize privacy loss over repeated queries, and even identical values of $\varepsilon$ may represent different guarantees depending on the protected data unit, accounting horizon, and observable outputs. This survey critically examines how privacy accounting evolves from single-query generation to multi-query RAG systems. papers.title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition
papers.abstract: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. papers.title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement. papers.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. papers.title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. papers.title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
papers.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. papers.abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. papers.title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert DNS Exfiltration Baked Into the Weights of an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough. papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices enables personalized large language model (LLM) inference while preserving privacy. However, RAG's inherent length asymmetry makes the prefill phase the dominant bottleneck. While precomputing the KV caches offline alleviates the prefill cost on server systems, the multi-gigabyte caches over the narrow interconnect create a severe I/O wall for on-device systems. To mitigate this, we propose MemLLM, an end-to-end in-storage processing (ISP) architecture that executes the complete attention pipeline based on precomputed KV caches within the SSD. MemLLM utilizes per-channel accelerators to fully utilize the aggregated NAND channel bandwidth and accelerates all KV cache-related computations on the storage-side to minimize PCIe transfers. papers.title: NOMOS: Compiling Written Policies into Statically Verified Tool-Call Gates for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, often silently. Prior defenses hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier per action, or compile policies through heavyweight formal machinery. Naive compilation fails: extracted rules block the tool satisfying their own precondition, or read arguments their tool lacks. papers.title: CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly generate multiple retrieval actions jointly, while downstream systems often provide only one reward for the resulting set. Broadcasting this reward provides a valid score-function gradient estimator for the expected set-level objective, but does not determine a coalition-dependent within-set attribution. We introduce CASI (Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval), which constructs the missing counterfactual information through snapshot-grounded set intervention: generate and retrieve once, hold replayable snapshot components fixed, and evaluate alternative subsets under common conditions. papers.abstract: Banks rely on extensive internal policy frameworks to ensure that corporate lending decisions comply with regulatory requirements and internal risk standards. Reviewing loan applications against these policies is a largely manual and knowledge-intensive process, which can lead to overlooked policy violations or exceptions. This report presents a prototype of an LLM-based policy checker that automatically verifies loan applications against internal lending policies. The proposed approach follows a two-step architecture. First, compliance-relevant rules are automatically extracted from policy documents and converted into structured, machine-readable representations. papers.title: Explorer-Zero: Improving Self-Play for Long-Horizon Tasks with Decomposable Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer explores the environment, constructs tasks, and records intermediate and final states as verification targets. These checkpoints reward partial completion, while alternating proposer--solver training adapts the generated curriculum. papers.abstract: Questions about an agent's history often require aggregating events, which retrieval alone does not resolve. We combine source-preserving evidence access with executable aggregation. Trajectory Memory (TM) retains the original trajectory and constructs a source-addressable reading view at question time. TallyMem augments it with a reusable event ledger, model-generated event specifications and deterministic execution. With a commit-specific adaptation on 776 questions from 99 held-out MINTEval repositories, TallyMem raises Qwen3-32B exact match from 35.2% to 49.0%, a 13.8-point gain over TM; gains span 12.8-13.9 points across three readers. A controlled probe with event sets parsed independently from raw logs shows an 11.0-point gain, from 82.8% to 93.8%, without routing. On full AMA-Bench, the routed system yields a smaller 1.3-point gain, from 69.8% to 71.1%. These results support exec

papers.title: Definition Grounding in Theory-Level Auto-formalization
papers.abstract: LLM-based auto-formalization systems can now generate formally verified Lean code at unprecedented rates. However, a formalization advances mathematical research only when further mathematical results can be built on it, especially when its definitions and helper lemmas are general enough to be imported and used idiomatically. We propose definition grounding, where definition formalizations are continuously judged and revised, as a method to ensure formalization quality. We find that agents formalizing definitions from textbook text often produce definitions that later statements cannot use, and only 25%-50% of their definition sets are compatible with all later statements. However, clarifying the informal definitions can improve this rate up to 77.5% averaged over all models. Furthermore, stating a small set of basic properties without proving them can improve model judges' capability t

papers.title: PREFER: From Player Experience to Personalized Game Refinement
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) evaluate gameplay experience is important for using their feedback to guide game design. However, overall ratings alone provide limited insight into which aspects of experience are associated with these judgments and how they can inform concrete game changes. We introduce PREFER, a framework that uses a shared set of experience dimensions adapted from established psychometric questionnaires to benchmark how models evaluate gameplay and to guide persona-specific game refinement. Through these dimensions, we characterize the perspectives models offer as virtual playtesters by examining how their overall assessments relate to specific aspects of experience and to the gameplay they produce. To examine how the same dimensions can guide refinement for players with different preferences, we use personas to simulate distinct player profiles. For eac

papers.title: One Monitor Does Not Fit All: Formalism-Agnostic Runtime Verification for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems combine model decisions, mutable state, tool calls, and delegation to external agents. Monitoring them requires observations from different execution boundaries, while prevention requires control before an operation produces its effect. We present AgenticRV, a runtime-verification architecture that separates these boundaries from the monitoring formalism. Adapters emit canonical events; each monitor receives its own projection and abstraction; and a decision policy uses normalised verdicts to select a reaction supported by the responsible adapter. We formalise when observations suffice, monitor replacement preserves decisions, and blocking prevents unsafe effects. We also distinguish rejected attempts from completed effects, avoiding the assumption that a blocked request must leave every monitor in a permanent violation state. The Python implementation supports LangGra

papers.title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflo

papers.title: LabOPBench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Laboratory Decision Making
papers.abstract: Laboratory experiments involve more than following predefined protocols; they require adaptive decision-making as the experimental state changes. Existing scientific benchmarks rarely assess such evidence-based decisions in laboratory settings. Here we present LabOPBench, a multimodal benchmark of 756 expert-authored, independently reviewed questions in organic synthesis and materials science. Each item pairs laboratory evidence with procedural context and an open-ended judgment, evaluated using a question-specific scoring rubric. Eight multimodal models obtain overall normalized scores of 28.8-45.8%, leaving substantial room for improvement. On a controlled 100-question subset, the strongest models outperform undergraduate participants on average but remain below the average performance of PhD participants. Expert analysis of responses from the three leading models identifies Evidence M

papers.title: Learning Individual Scientific Taste with Privileged Hindsight Distillation
papers.abstract: Scientific taste shapes which research directions researchers pursue, and it varies across individuals. Existing work evaluates research directions along multiple evaluation criteria or models scientific taste using community feedback signals such as citations and reviews, but neither directly captures how individuals translate assessments under the same criteria into different preferences. We model scientific taste as a researcher-specific mapping from criterion-level assessments in a shared, evidence-grounded evaluation space with proposal-visible evidence, to relative preferences. A population-level mapping learned from retrospective supervision provides a cold start when individual feedback is scarce. We introduce Privileged Hindsight Distillation (PHD), which uses later-emerging scientific evidence during training to improve proposal-time criterion assessment and the population mapp

papers.title: What Coding Agents Leave Unsaid: Measuring Task-State Gaps Between Execution and Reports
papers.abstract: Human supervisors rely on coding agents' reports to assess progress, verify repairs, and decide when to intervene. But a supervisor cannot investigate a failure they were never told occurred. Failed attempts, workarounds, and unresolved risks may disappear from routine reports, leaving supervisors unaware of issues that warrant scrutiny. We conduct CTXGAP, a measurement study quantifying the gap in task-state recoverability between agents' accumulated user-facing reports and their full recorded execution contexts. Across 37 coding tasks and 4,799 valid probes, agents answer 93.6% of task-state questions on demand; full-context readers recover 92.7%, while report-only readers recover 52.0%, a 40.7-point gap. At the final checkpoints of 30 verified fixes, the gap remains 34.8 points. Human annotation identifies states mentioned without enough supporting detail as the largest category of un

papers.title: When Protection Overrides Consequences: Understanding Protection Mode in Large Language Model Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. At lowest effort, at least one of four responses prioritizes the subject on 34.74% of Sol prompts and over 83% of MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-27B prompts; none of four independent human raters does so. Controls show that choices usually track physical risk. We elicit both risks before requesting an action. Some models assess risk incorrectly; others state the correct ordering but still choose the subject. Qwen3.5-27B with thinking shows 100% correct risk ordering but 57.81% subject choice among eligible conversations on eight selected scene

papers.title: Plant Memory: Technical Language Processing and a Verified Maintenance Ontology for Agent-Accessible Failure Knowledge from SAP PM Work Orders
papers.abstract: Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, yet in most plants they are close to unusable for analysis. Short texts are abbreviated and misspelt, asset identity is buried in free text, work-type labels contradict the work described, and the fields that matter most for reliability (symptom, root cause, action taken) are usually empty. As a result, diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians and leaves when they do. We present Plant Memory, a system that applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224-aligned maintenance ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, the evidence it was read from, and a verification state. Extraction is rule-first, with an optional large language model (LLM) acting as a second reader whose disagreements

papers.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. papers.title: The Wealth of Agents: Scaling Agentic AI Across Developers
papers.abstract: Today's agentic systems are typically designed, built, and deployed by single developers with full control over all participating agents. While this simplifies development, it limits the potential scale of agentic systems. We study multi-developer agentic systems (MDAs) which enable developers to collaboratively build agentic systems to push frontier capability beyond what any individual developer could achieve alone. We construct empirical and theoretical models of developers to compare MDAs with single-developer agentic systems (SDAs). On GAIA, a general assistant benchmark, a population of specialized developers whose individual agents do not exceed 35% accuracy reaches 70% when their agents are combined in an MDA. This MDA performs 12 percentage points above the median general-purpose SDA built with several times each specialist's development budget. Our theoretical models show how M

papers.title: Graph-Based Orchestration of Heterogeneous AI Models: A Control Node Approach to Composite Intelligence
papers.abstract: We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

papers.title: Robust Counterfactuals for Markov Decision Processes under Statistical and Causal Uncertainties
papers.abstract: Counterfactual reasoning (asking what would have happened, had a decision been different) is a powerful tool for identifying causes of failure and explaining the behaviour of AI systems in sequential decision-making tasks. In Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), two sources of uncertainty complicate counterfactual inference: statistical uncertainty in the MDP transitions when the MDP is estimated from trajectory data, and uncertainty about the unknown causal model, as there are multiple structural causal models (SCMs) compatible with each MDP. Existing work addresses these two challenges in isolation. We address both simultaneously by introducing a framework for partial counterfactual inference in MDPs that is robust to both statistical and causal uncertainty. Our approach provides: 1) closed-form analytical bounds for the counterfactual probabilities that are valid across all SCMs entailed

papers.title: Sparse Transformer: a Controlled Testbed for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to decompose neural network computations into human-understandable features, yet progress is limited by the absence of ground-truth units to evaluate against. We address this with a Sparse Transformer (ST): a 5-layer language model trained on TinyStories whose wide, TopK-sparse MLP forces neuron specialization. We show that ST neurons are highly interpretable: they outperform a loss-matched dense transformer by 43% on AutoInterp, and circuits of a median of 12 neurons suffice to reproduce individual model predictions. This testbed allows us to directly compare feature learning methods: Transcoder, which approximates the MLP input-output mapping, recovers ST's neuron vectors with 52.6% higher cosine similarity than Sparse Autoencoder, which only reconstructs outputs. Furthermore, the ST enables a controlled study of polysemanticity: distilling its sparse

papers.title: DANGERLENS: Probing Dangerous Representations Hidden by Safety Alignment
papers.abstract: Safety alignment teaches language models to refuse harmful requests, yet the internal accessibility of hazardous concepts can retain traces of earlier training. Can checkpoints with equally safe behavior differ in what remains accessible behind their refusals? In this work, we investigate this question through paired training histories and a direct audit of intermediate representations. We introduce DANGERLENS, a probe that maps hidden states into vocabulary space and uses blinded semantic judgments to distinguish harmful goals and operational means from hazard recognition and safety control. Experiments on three Qwen1.5 scales show that checkpoints with prior harmful exposure generally retain greater hazardous concept accessibility after the same safety alignment, with the strongest separation in intermediate and later layers. The same harmful update also produces different behavioral t

papers.title: Whose turn is it? Context-guided model routing for stateful agents
papers.abstract: Model routing can reduce the cost of LLM applications by assigning simpler requests to cheaper models without sacrificing the quality of the response. However, most routers treat requests as independent. Stateful agents do not operate under this assumption: a user turn may require multiple model and tool calls, its difficulty depends on the state produced by earlier turns, and changing models can sacrifice reuse of the conversational prompt cache. We study zero-shot, cost-aware routing at the user-turn boundary, systematically varying the routing rule, access to session history, candidate models that differ in size, reasoning effort, or model provider, and prompt-cache behavior. We evaluate on multi-turn versions of SheetCopilot and SpreadsheetBench 2, where persistent workbooks and cross-turn dependencies make isolated routing decisions especially brittle. At a matched offloading rate,

papers.title: MemeTrace: A Multimodal LLM-Based Agent for Safety-Aware Meme Provenance Analysis
papers.abstract: Online memes are often carriers of unsafe content such as disinformation and propaganda. Their rapid evolution in response to news events and strong dependence on contextual information make it difficult for platforms and moderators to detect and moderate them effectively. Moreover, existing moderation studies typically classify memes as safe or unsafe based on individual images, lacking the ability to perform broader provenance analysis, i.e., where a meme originates, how it spreads, what cultural symbolism it represents, whether it poses potential risks to society, etc. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemeTrace, a multimodal LLM-based agent that automatically traces the provenance and potential risks of emerging memes. We evaluate MemeTrace on Meme100, a dataset of 100 real-world memes, using both human annotation and automatic metrics. The results demonstrate that MemeTrace substanti

papers.title: AgentCIScope: Grounded Contextual Integrity Evaluation for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents are becoming increasingly capable of handling daily workspace tasks by interacting with application environments through tool calls. However, as agents read and write sensitive user data across email, documents, and other applications, a central privacy question is whether they preserve contextual integrity (CI), that is, whether the information flows they produce comply with context-specific disclosure constraints. Existing work either focuses on model-level privacy leakage or evaluates agents in limited application environments with manually constructed disclosure constraints. In this work, we introduce AgentCIScope, a unified platform and benchmark for evaluating agent-level contextual integrity through executable, multi-step tasks across diverse, realistic application environments. AgentCIScope transforms public and synthetic privacy cases into executable agent tasks, with

papers.title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest

papers.title: Are You Reading the Right Thing? Rethinking Internal Signals for Prompt-Injection Detection
papers.abstract: Several recent studies propose detecting prompt injections from a language model's internal state. However, these methods do not measure a single security property. Residual-stream probes, attention scores, role projections, exposure probes, and concept readouts may capture injection presence, recognition, information routing, or behavioral influence. It is therefore unclear what differences in prompt-injection detection performance reveal about the internal signals these methods read. We study how five representation-reading methods vary under a common structured indirect prompt-injection setup on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. We evaluate each method by how well it distinguishes injected prompts from benign controls. We then further analyze each detection method's ability to detect attacks in cases where they are successful and in cases where they are not. This helps us better

papers.title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It combines verifiable subtask outcome scoring with evidence-supported multi-judge trajectory evaluation and distills phase-level bottlenecks, success patterns, and failure patterns into diagnostic feedback for generating new executable tasks. Across two rounds of cybersecurity experiments, evaluations of eight models on 66 tasks reveal phase-level performance differences and common failure patterns

papers.title: ixi-sLM: On-Device sLM for AI Call Agent Service
papers.abstract: Running an AI call agent on-device makes it private, network-independent, and free of per-query cloud cost, but shipping one as a real-world service imposes constraints a cloud deployment never faces: ~1GiB memory budget, in-call latency and thermal limits, static-integer NPU execution, Korean STT input far from sLM pretraining, and cloud-level quality expectations. We bring ixi-sLM, a 1.2B Korean sLM, to mobile NPUs through ON-DEVICE MODELING: domain-adaptive modeling trims the vocabulary by call frequency to shrink the embedding and LM head that take nearly half the model under INT4 transformer weights and refits the tokenizer to call speech (18% fewer tokens on call traffic), while task-aware quantization calibrates on real calls and assigns per-module mixed precision by activation sensitivity. A single domain-adapted model runs ixi-O's two production services, AI Call Summary and AI

papers.title: Argument Graph Uncertainty: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Logical Structure of Reasoning Chains
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying large language models in high-stakes reasoning tasks, yet most existing approaches rely on expensive sampling strategies or shallow token-level signals that ignore the internal logical structure of model outputs. We introduce Argument Graph Uncertainty, a post-hoc framework for multiple choice question tasks, that estimates model confidence directly from the logical structure of a single chain-of-thought reasoning trace. Our method uses either a lightweight instruction-tuned model or a simple deterministic rule to segment the reasoning chain into propositional units, then applies a NLI model to infer relational edges and construct two complementary argument graphs over these segments. papers.title: LabCompiler: A Framework for Verifiable Human-Machine Laboratory Execution from Imperfect Protocols
papers.abstract: Closing the loop of AI-driven science requires reliably translating natural-language protocols into executable laboratory workflows despite protocol defects and heterogeneous hardware. Existing approaches often couple scientific interpretation with device-specific code generation, making errors difficult to localize and limiting reuse across laboratory platforms. We introduce LabCompiler, a robust protocol-to-execution framework that transforms imperfect natural-language protocols into verifiable human-machine workflows. Its protocol firewall diagnoses and repairs defects before compilation while preserving unaffected content, guided by troubleshooting knowledge accumulated through perturbation-guided self-evolution. papers.title: MemCode: Discrete Semantic Representations for Long-Term Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Long-term memory remains a fundamental bottleneck for large language model (LLM) agents across sessions. Existing systems typically adopt a write-then-retrieve paradigm, storing context-dependent dialogue fragments and retrieving them via nearest-neighbor search in a continuous embedding space. This design yields unstable access units and systematically misses logically related but lexically distant evidence. We propose MemCode, a long-term agent memory framework that couples retrieval-oriented writing with discrete associative retrieval. MemCode rewrites dialogue into self-contained atomic memory units (AMUs), maps AMUs into a learnable codebook with isomorphic semantic quantization (ISQ), and uses codebook co-occurrence topology as a retrieval path complementary to vector search. For long-term memory stores, MemCode separates online atomic writes from asynchronous offline consolidation

papers.title: ActiveEvidence: Decision-Focused Evidence Graphs with Verifiable Acquisition Gaps
papers.abstract: A multimodal agent must decide whether visual evidence is worth acquiring, which candidate or resolution to query, and when further interaction can no longer change its decision. We study this problem under a strict free-metadata/paid-observation boundary, stochastic vector costs, and a frozen execution trace, and treat it as decision-certifiable active evidence acquisition. A Counterfactual Evidence Interaction Graph (CEIG) represents unary evidence value, signed second-order interaction, and directed conditional harm while maintaining explicit score enclosures for unresolved interactions; a decision-weighted enclosure objective tightens the bounds that can change action identity. papers.title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are har

papers.title: CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code-switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. This context-sensitive ability remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce CSWBench, a benchmark for evaluating context-sensitive code-switching in creative writing through two complementary settings: Focused Narrative and Extended Narrative. We further propose CSWEval, a theory-informed framework with two complementary levels: event-level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole-text evaluation of task-specific quality---overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extend

papers.title: ACR-Net: Mitigating Semantic Dominance via Contrastive Acoustic-Semantic Decoupling
papers.abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) models and Audio LLMs fail when vocal tone contradicts textual semantics. Extensive training on congruent data engenders a rigid semantic prior, causing "Semantic Dominance", a severe text bias during cross-modal conflicts. We introduce the ASPIRE benchmark of adversarial audio-text pairs across four conflict types, alongside two metrics: Semantic Overconfidence Penalty (SOP) and Latent Decoupling Degree (LDD). Unlike fusion methods that merely re-weight collapsed features, our Acoustic Conflict Resolution Network (ACR-Net) uses Cross-Modal Attention and Contrastive Decoupling Loss to disentangle contradictory representations into orthogonal latent spaces. Experiments show existing models fail under polarity conflicts due to extreme semantic overconfidence. papers.title: Provable Transformer Context Compression for In-Context Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $Θ(γ^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-γ))\})$ where $γ$ is the discounting factor

papers.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
papers.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. papers.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://g

papers.title: FUSE: Fairness-aware Update Screening against Byzantine Exploitation in $q$-Fair Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Client-level fair federated learning, in the form of $q$-fair federated learning ($q$-FFL), agnostic federated learning, or tilted empirical risk minimization, has emerged as an attractive solution to equalize utility across heterogeneous clients. This paradigm grants high-loss clients greater relative influence, while a central server aggregates their loss-weighted updates into a single shared model. Yet, the Byzantine robustness of $q$-fair federated learning has been largely neglected, leaving the server unable to tell legitimate fairness-induced amplification from malicious update scaling. To address this critical gap, we formalize the problem of Byzantine-robust $q$-fair federated learning under an \emph{update-only interface}, in which the server observes nothing but the fairness-scaled client updates. Our analysis under shared class-conditional label skew shows that fairness scali

papers.title: Beyond Equation Search: Conjecture-Guided Discovery with SCOPE and ClosureBench
papers.abstract: Most symbolic regression methods optimize candidate equations, but improving an equation's fit does not establish whether its underlying scientific conjecture should be retained, revised, or rejected. A conjecture may admit multiple mathematical realizations, and similarly accurate equations may imply different explanations. This motivates a shift from refining individual expressions to developing and testing the conjectures that guide them. We introduce SCOPE, a framework that sustains multiple conjecture-driven research trajectories. Multiple scientist agents independently pursue conjectures through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise their conjectures and research directions. papers.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection.
